title: A hundred dear, a hundred sorrows
hookLine: Visakha grieves a grandchild; how many would you want to love?

cards: Visakha comes to the Buddha in the middle of the day, her clothes wet, her hair wet. A granddaughter she dearly loved has died. The text doesn't say why she's wet; some readers take it as the washing after a funeral.

Visakha is a lay follower the early texts honor for her generosity; tradition says she built a monastery in Savatthi. Why have you come here at midday, the Buddha asks, with your clothes and hair wet? She tells him.
And he answers with a question.

teach.h: AS MANY AS LIVE IN SAVATTHI?
teach.b: Visakha, he asks, would you like to have as many children and grandchildren as there are people in Savatthi? Yes, she says. And how many people die in Savatthi each day?
Ten, she says, or nine, or five, or one.

teach.h: NEVER A DAY WITHOUT A DEATH.
teach.b: Savatthi is never without someone dying. Then, he says, would you ever be without wet clothes and wet hair? No, she says.
Enough with so many. Then the Buddha says it plainly: those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows. Those who have ninety have ninety.

And so on, down to one: one dear, one sorrow. Those who have none dear have no sorrow. Then the verse: grief and lamentation and all the many kinds of suffering in the world exist because of what is dear.
Where there's nothing dear, they don't. You may remember Kisa Gotami from the first year, and not long ago, the dart of grief. This is the same teaching from another side.
Notice how he does it. He doesn't tell Visakha her grief is a mistake. He lets her do the arithmetic herself.
Buddhist teachers read the line in more than one way.

teach.h: A HUNDRED DEAR, A HUNDRED SORROWS.
teach.b: Some say it's about clinging, holding the dear as mine, not about ceasing to love; the same canon praises boundless kindness to all. Others hear in it the monk's path of renunciation.

how: Visakha is honored in Theravada tradition as a model lay disciple, and teachers sometimes tell her story alongside Kisa Gotami's when speaking about grief.

games.q: a hundred dear: tap the pairs.
p: came at midday, clothes and hair wet
never a day without a death

s: the Buddha told Visakha her grief was a mistake
he asked her questions and let her work out the arithmetic herself.
Visakha first said she'd like as many grandchildren as there are people in Savatthi
then she saw she would never be without mourning.
all Buddhist teachers read this as a call to stop loving
some read it as about clinging; the same canon praises boundless kindness.

games.q: you're Visakha. the Buddha asks if you'd like as many grandchildren as there are people in Savatthi. you've said yes. then he asks how many people die there each day. what do you see?
o: that you'd have more joy than sorrow.
that you'd never be without wet clothes and hair.
that the question doesn't apply to you.
games.why: she sees she would always be mourning someone, and says, enough. then the Buddha names the teaching: a hundred dear, a hundred sorrows.

practice: Bring to mind one person you love, and feel how dear they are. If an edge of fear comes with it, that they might be hurt, or leave, or die, notice it gently; that's the sorrow the Buddha was counting.
Don't push the love away; just loosen your grip a little, the way you'd hold a bird: close enough to keep it warm, open enough to let it breathe.

wordCard.voice: Soka, sorrow. The Buddha's words to the grieving Visakha: a hundred dear ones, a hundred sorrows; one dear, one sorrow. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali soka: sorrow, grief. in Udana 8.8's verse, sorrow and lamentation arise because of what is dear.

carryVoice: Your line: with an open hand. The Buddha let Visakha do the arithmetic herself. Day six hundred twenty-two, done.
